+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }
+

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

   \phi=\sum_{\rho\in\Irr(G)}

+# Tier-2 literature audit
+
+Search date: 2026-08-14. Sources checked: arXiv API and full texts, Crossref
+DOI metadata, zbMATH Open API, and the open-problem sections of the cited
+papers. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex API calls returned HTTP 429, so they
+did not supply affirmative status evidence. Exact-title and exact-phrase
+searches located no later paper claiming to resolve the four questions below;
+they are therefore treated as open, not as proved unresolved by this audit.
+The later arXiv papers found for linear Mahler equations (arXiv:2308.16765,
+2412.04928, and 2503.12995) concern twisted summability or Hahn-series
+solutions and do not claim the all-parameter polynomial-time bound in item 3.
+
+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }
+

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

 \[
   \phi=\sum_{\rho\in\Irr(G)}

+# Tier-2 literature audit
+
+Search date: 2026-08-14. Sources checked: arXiv API and full texts, Crossref
+DOI metadata, zbMATH Open API, and the open-problem sections of the cited
+papers. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex API calls returned HTTP 429, so they
+did not supply affirmative status evidence. Exact-title and exact-phrase
+searches located no later paper claiming to resolve the four questions below;
+they are therefore treated as open, not as proved unresolved by this audit.
+The later arXiv papers found for linear Mahler equations (arXiv:2308.16765,
+2412.04928, and 2503.12995) concern twisted summability or Hahn-series
+solutions and do not claim the all-parameter polynomial-time bound in item 3.
+
+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }
+

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

 \[
   \phi=\sum_{\rho\in\Irr(G)}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

For arbitrary binary extensions on one \(v\)-vertex base, fewer than
\(16v^3\) algebraic radial samples in the open Perron interval determine the
complete primitive length--class profile; the strict twisted gap is needed
only if the Perron endpoint is sampled.  The determinant ratio governing the
test is canonically the ratio of the standard Artin--Mazur zeta functions of
the two binary covers.  The proof is genuinely effective:
one collision produces a unique rational Mahler certificate, its numerator
and denominator satisfy explicit input-dependent degree and height bounds,
and a finite Pad\'e system reconstructs or rejects it.  The exact four-vertex
pair shows why a single Perron-boundary value cannot be an inverse invariant.

The strongest implication in this chain is the determinant lifting theorem.
Its interior form is unconditional, while its endpoint form uses the strict
gap only to continue through the Perron circle.  The arithmetic proof uses
more than positivity of a rational function:
same-base determinant parity supplies integral coefficients for the critical
Mahler product, Nishioka's theorem converts an algebraic special value into
algebraicity of the function, and the explicit algebraic-to-rational descent
then supplies the coboundary.  Removing the parity hypothesis would require a
different arithmetic input.

The same mechanism does not presently yield a polynomial sample bound for
every finite group.  For \(C_3\), Adams--M\"obius inversion already couples
two character determinants at infinitely many arithmetically distributed
powers, rather than one lacunary Mahler orbit.  A general finite-group theorem
therefore requires a new special-value and effective zero theory for these
coupled Euler systems.  In its absence, the proved general statement remains
unconditional analytic recovery from a profile set with an interior
accumulation point.

+# Tier-2 literature audit
+
+Search date: 2026-08-14. Sources checked: arXiv API and full texts, Crossref
+DOI metadata, zbMATH Open API, and the open-problem sections of the cited
+papers. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex API calls returned HTTP 429, so they
+did not supply affirmative status evidence. Exact-title and exact-phrase
+searches located no later paper claiming to resolve the four questions below;
+they are therefore treated as open, not as proved unresolved by this audit.
+The later arXiv papers found for linear Mahler equations (arXiv:2308.16765,
+2412.04928, and 2503.12995) concern twisted summability or Hahn-series
+solutions and do not claim the all-parameter polynomial-time bound in item 3.
+
+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }
+

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

For arbitrary binary extensions on one \(v\)-vertex base, fewer than
\(16v^3\) algebraic radial samples in the open Perron interval determine the
complete primitive length--class profile; the strict twisted gap is needed
only if the Perron endpoint is sampled.  The determinant ratio governing the
test is canonically the ratio of the standard Artin--Mazur zeta functions of
the two binary covers.  The proof is genuinely effective:
one collision produces a unique rational Mahler certificate, its numerator
and denominator satisfy explicit input-dependent degree and height bounds,
and a finite Pad\'e system reconstructs or rejects it.  The exact four-vertex
pair shows why a single Perron-boundary value cannot be an inverse invariant.

The strongest implication in this chain is the determinant lifting theorem.
Its interior form is unconditional, while its endpoint form uses the strict
gap only to continue through the Perron circle.  The arithmetic proof uses
more than positivity of a rational function:
same-base determinant parity supplies integral coefficients for the critical
Mahler product, Nishioka's theorem converts an algebraic special value into
algebraicity of the function, and the explicit algebraic-to-rational descent
then supplies the coboundary.  Removing the parity hypothesis would require a
different arithmetic input.

The same mechanism does not presently yield a polynomial sample bound for
every finite group.  For \(C_3\), Adams--M\"obius inversion already couples
two character determinants at infinitely many arithmetically distributed
powers, rather than one lacunary Mahler orbit.  A general finite-group theorem
therefore requires a new special-value and effective zero theory for these
coupled Euler systems.  In its absence, the proved general statement remains
unconditional analytic recovery from a profile set with an interior
accumulation point.

1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."

   \(\mathbb ZG\)."

3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the

   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
   well."

## Machinery map

- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
  answer either problem.
- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
  or Markov maps.

## A/B/C/D audit

- A: none of the named problems is solved.
- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+# Tier-2 literature audit
+
+Search date: 2026-08-14. Sources checked: arXiv API and full texts, Crossref
+DOI metadata, zbMATH Open API, and the open-problem sections of the cited
+papers. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex API calls returned HTTP 429, so they
+did not supply affirmative status evidence. Exact-title and exact-phrase
+searches located no later paper claiming to resolve the four questions below;
+they are therefore treated as open, not as proved unresolved by this audit.
+The later arXiv papers found for linear Mahler equations (arXiv:2308.16765,
+2412.04928, and 2503.12995) concern twisted summability or Hahn-series
+solutions and do not claim the all-parameter polynomial-time bound in item 3.
+
+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

\begin{theorem}[Interior determinant lifting and endpoint extension]
\label{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting}
Let \(A\) be a primitive non-negative integer matrix with Perron root
\(\lambda>1\), and put \(x=\lambda^{-1}\).  Let \(B,B'\) be integer matrices
of the same size such that, entrywise,
\[
 \abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij},
 \qquad B_{ij}\equiv B'_{ij}\equiv A_{ij}\pmod2,
\]
and set
\[
 H(z)=\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}.
\]
For every algebraic number \(y\) with \(0<y<x\), the following are
equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
 \item \(\Pi_y(H)=1\);
 \item there is a unique \(R\in\QQ(z)^\times\) such that
 \[
  R(0)=R(y)=1,
  \qquad H(z)=\frac{R(z^2)}{R(z)^2}.
 \]
\end{enumerate}
If \(\rad(B),\rad(B')<\lambda\), the equivalence also holds at \(y=x\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The Perron-weighted norm estimate in the proof of
\Cref{lem:perron-weighted-domination}, now using
\(\abs{B_{ij}},\abs{B'_{ij}}\le A_{ij}\), gives
\(\rad(B),\rad(B')\le\lambda\).  If \(y<x\), choose
\(r\) with \(y<r<x\); if \(y=x\) and both strict gaps hold, choose \(r\) with
\(x<r<1\) below both reciprocal spectral radii.  In either case both determinant
polynomials are non-zero on \(\abs z<r\).  They are real, non-zero on
\([0,y]\), and equal one at zero, so they are positive there and \(H>0\) on
that interval.  Define \(F\) by \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-product}.  By
\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, it is analytic on \(\abs z<r\), has
integer coefficients, and satisfies \eqref{eq:critical-mahler-equation}.
Crucially, the product normalization is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
 F(y)^2=\Pi_y(H),
\end{equation}
not \(F(y)=\Pi_y(H)\).

We now verify every hypothesis of Nishioka's special-value theorem
\cite[Theorem, p.~387]{Nishioka1982MahlerFunctionValues}.  Write the rational
function \(H\) in reduced form
\[
 H=\frac{\widehat P_0}{\widehat P_1},
 \qquad
 \widehat P_0,\widehat P_1\in\ZZ[z],
 \qquad
 \gcd(\widehat P_0,\widehat P_1)=1,
 \qquad
 \widehat P_0(0)=\widehat P_1(0)=1.
\]
The common factors removed here do not affect zero-freeness on \(\abs z<r\).
In the notation of the cited theorem, take
\[
 Tz=z^2,
 \qquad
 Q_0(z,u)=\widehat P_0(z),
 \qquad
 Q_1(z,u)=-\widehat P_1(z)u^2.
\]
Then the functional equation is exactly
\[
 Q_0(z,F(z))F(Tz)+Q_1(z,F(z))=0.
\]
The two polynomials \(Q_0,Q_1\) are relatively prime in
\(\overline{\QQ}[z,u]\): a common factor cannot contain \(u\), since
\(\widehat P_0(0)=1\), and the remaining assertion is the displayed
coprimality of \(\widehat P_0,\widehat P_1\).  Nishioka's auxiliary
polynomial \(g(z)\), obtained as a polynomial combination of the \(Q_i\)
and independent of \(u\), may therefore be chosen simply as
\(g(z)=Q_0(z,u)=\widehat P_0(z)\).

The numerical parameters are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
  p&=2, & N&=0, & n&=1, & m&=2,\\
  M&=\max\{p+N,m\}=2, & U&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(m\) is the maximum \(u\)-degree of the \(Q_i\), exactly as in the
printed definition; that theorem permits both \(N=0\) and \(L=1\).
Thus, with coefficient-growth exponent \(L=1\), her strict inequality is
\[
 M(p+N)n^2=2\cdot2\cdot1=4
 <2^{2+1/L}=8.
\]
It remains to check the arithmetic and orbit conditions, rather than merely
record the parameters.  Write \(F(z)=\sum_{h\ge0}a_hz^h\).  By
\Cref{lem:critical-mahler-integrality}, all \(a_h\) lie in the fixed number
field \(\QQ\) and are algebraic integers.  Choose \(s\) with \(y<s<r\).
Cauchy's estimate on \(\abs z=s\) gives
\[
  \abs{a_h}\le \max_{\abs z=s}\abs{F(z)}\,s^{-h}.
\]
Hence Nishioka's coefficient-size and common-denominator bounds hold with
\(L=1\): the denominators are one and the logarithmic coefficient height is
at most linear in \(h\).  The evaluation point \(y\) is a non-zero algebraic
number and \(0<Uy<1\).  Moreover,
\[
 T^i y=y^{2^i}\ne0,
 \qquad
 g(T^i y)=\widehat P_0(y^{2^i})\ne0
 \quad(i\ge0),
\]
because \(0<y^{2^i}\le y<r\) and the reduced numerator is zero-free
on \(\abs z<r\).  Finally \(F(y)\) converges because \(F\) is analytic
there.
All hypotheses of the cited theorem are therefore satisfied.  It follows
that if \(F\) were transcendental over \(\CC(z)\), then \(F(y)\) would be
transcendental.

Assume \(\textup{(i)}\).  Positivity and \eqref{eq:critical-product-square-normalization}
give \(F(y)=1\), so the cited theorem forces \(F\) to be algebraic.  By
\Cref{prop:algebraic-mahler-coboundary}, \(H=\delta R\) for the unique
normalized rational \(R\).  Now
\Cref{prop:rational-mahler-certificate} gives
\(1=\Pi_y(H)=R(y)^{-2}\) and \(R(y)>0\), hence \(R(y)=1\).  This proves
\(\textup{(ii)}\).  Conversely, \(\textup{(ii)}\) and
\eqref{eq:rational-mahler-telescope} give \(\textup{(i)}\), and the
same proposition gives uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the lifting theorem]
The determinant parity in \Cref{thm:determinant-boundary-lifting} is essential
to the integrality step, so the theorem does not assert the converse for an
arbitrary positive rational \(H\).  Its realizable class is nevertheless broad.
Fix \(r\ge2\), an odd \(a>0\), and a positive even \(b\), and let \(A\) have
diagonal entries \(a\) and off-diagonal entries \(b\).  Then
\(\lambda=a+(r-1)b\).  Any diagonal \(B=\operatorname{diag}(c_i)\) and
\(B'=\operatorname{diag}(d_i)\), with odd
\(\abs{c_i},\abs{d_i}\le a\), satisfies the same-base compatibility and
strict gaps, and realizes
\[
 H(z)=\frac{\prod_i(1-c_i z)}{\prod_i(1-d_i z)}.
\]
\end{remark}

The preceding lifting theorem supplies a rational certificate abstractly.  We
now show that its existence and the certificate itself are decidable by a
single finite Pad\'e calculation.  For an integral polynomial \(P\), write

+# Tier-2 literature audit
+
+Search date: 2026-08-14. Sources checked: arXiv API and full texts, Crossref
+DOI metadata, zbMATH Open API, and the open-problem sections of the cited
+papers. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex API calls returned HTTP 429, so they
+did not supply affirmative status evidence. Exact-title and exact-phrase
+searches located no later paper claiming to resolve the four questions below;
+they are therefore treated as open, not as proved unresolved by this audit.
+The later arXiv papers found for linear Mahler equations (arXiv:2308.16765,
+2412.04928, and 2503.12995) concern twisted summability or Hahn-series
+solutions and do not claim the all-parameter polynomial-time bound in item 3.
+
+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

**Outcome**

The paper does not solve a named open problem. I integrated a genuine route-(C) hypothesis removal and a route-(B) identification with standard dynamical zeta functions. Full sources and search records are in the [literature audit](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/artifacts/tier2_literature_audit.md:1).

**Named Problems**

1. Boyle–Schmieding, “Finite group extensions of shifts of finite type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic,” ETDS 37 (2017), DOI `10.1017/etds.2015.87`, Realization Problem 6.1(2): “Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\).”
Mapping: our determinant lifting theorem analyzes already-realized same-base matrices; it does not characterize positivity or realizability.

2. Boyle–Schmieding, ibid., Problem 6.1(3): “Given a finite group \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\).”
Mapping: our Fourier and primitive-orbit formulas recover realized trace/class data but supply no necessary-and-sufficient realization criterion.

3. Chyzak–Dreyfus–Dumas–Mezzarobba, “Computing solutions of linear Mahler equations,” Math. Comp. 87 (2018), DOI `10.1090/mcom/3359`, §4.3: “This result leaves open the question of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations that run in polynomial time in \(r\) and \(d\), for all possible combinations of these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the equation is zero.”
Mapping: our finite Padé algorithm handles one normalized nonlinear order-one coboundary equation, not arbitrary linear Mahler equations or all order-degree regimes.

4. O’Hare, “Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps,” ETDS 45 (2025), DOI `10.1017/etds.2024.83`, Introduction: “It would be interesting to study finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as well.”
Mapping: our theorem concerns symbolic orbit-class Euler values, not periodic derivative data; no distortion or coding argument transfers it to O’Hare’s setting.

Searches covered arXiv/full texts, Crossref, zbMATH, later Mahler papers, and printed open-problem sections. Exact-title and phrase searches found no resolution; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429, so “still open” is the best-supported status, not a proof of non-resolution.

**B/C/D Audit And Result**

B: the binary determinant ratio is now proved to be canonically
\[
\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}=
\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}{\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)},
\]
a ratio of standard Artin–Mazur zeta functions of two-sheeted SFT covers; see [the proposition](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/sec_refocused_framework.tex:175).

C was chosen for the best success-impact product. Entrywise domination proves \(\rho(B),\rho(B')\leq\lambda\), so for every algebraic \(0<y<\lambda^{-1}\), the collision condition is equivalent to a unique rational Mahler certificate without any strict twisted gap; see [the lifting theorem](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/sec_refocused_boundary_collisions.tex:451).

Consequently, fewer than \(16v^3\) interior algebraic samples recover every binary primitive length-class profile unconditionally. General finite-group recovery from any radial set with an interior accumulation point is also unconditional. The strict gap remains only for evaluating at \(y=\lambda^{-1}\).

The parity hypothesis remains real: it supplies integral Mahler coefficients required by the special-value argument. For \(C_3\), Adams–Möbius inversion couples character determinants at non-lacunary powers, precisely where the one-function Mahler method stops.

D offers no tier-raising result: the cubic sample bound has no matching lower bound, and the four-vertex construction proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient. No sharp converse or optimal constant was established.

**Verification And Tier**

The strengthened [verifier](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/artifacts/verify_a5_results.py:651) derives the common base, twisted blocks, covers, zeta identity, spectral radii, and all-scale dyadic sign certificate. All 26 unit tests passed; the standalone verifier ended `STATUS: PASS`.

`latexmk -pdfxe -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error main.tex` exited 0 after a forced rebuild: 28 pages, no undefined references/citations, LaTeX errors, or overfull boxes; two harmless underfull-box warnings remain. `git diff --check -- .` found no whitespace errors. No `pytest`, commit, or unrelated-file modification was performed.

Honest ceiling: upper Tier-3 / specialist Tier-2 boundary. ETDS is plausible but not secured; JFA, Trans. AMS, and Math. Comp. are not justified without solving one of the named realization/rigidity problems or proving a genuinely sharp sampling theorem.

+1. M. Boyle and S. Schmieding, *Finite group extensions of shifts of finite
+   type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic*, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 37 (2017),
+   1026-1059, DOI 10.1017/etds.2015.87, Realization Problem 6.1(2):
+   "Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials
+   \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+2. Boyle-Schmieding, ibid., Realization Problem 6.1(3): "Given a finite group
+   \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series
+   \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over
+   \(\mathbb ZG\)."
+
+3. F. Chyzak, T. Dreyfus, P. Dumas, and M. Mezzarobba, *Computing solutions
+   of linear Mahler equations*, Math. Comp. 87 (2018), 2977-3021,
+   DOI 10.1090/mcom/3359, Section 4.3: "This result leaves open the question
+   of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations
+   that run in polynomial time in r and d, for all possible combinations of
+   these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the
+   equation is zero."
+
+4. T. A. O'Hare, *Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps*,
+   Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 45 (2025), 1597-1618,
+   DOI 10.1017/etds.2024.83, Introduction: "It would be interesting to study
+   finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as
+   well."
+
+## Machinery map
+
+- Problems 1-2: the manuscript computes the realized determinant and
+  conjugate trace data and proves their equivalence to primitive class data.
+  It does not characterize positivity/realizability and therefore does not
+  answer either problem.
+- Problem 3: Theorem `thm:effective-rational-mahler-coboundary` gives a
+  polynomial-time finite Pade test for one normalized nonlinear order-one
+  coboundary equation. It does not cover arbitrary linear Mahler order and
+  degree or a vanishing trailing coefficient.
+- Problem 4: Theorem `thm:finite-radial-sampling` is exact finite-data
+  recovery for a Markov symbolic model. Its data are class Euler values, not
+  periodic derivatives, and no distortion estimate transfers it to unimodal
+  or Markov maps.
+
+## A/B/C/D audit
+
+- A: none of the named problems is solved.
+- B: Proposition `prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio` canonically identifies the
+  binary determinant ratio with a ratio of ordinary Artin-Mazur zeta
+  functions of standard two-sheeted covers.
+- C: Theorems `thm:determinant-boundary-lifting`,
+  `thm:finite-radial-sampling`, and `thm:radial-profile-recovery` no longer
+  assume a strict twisted gap in the open Perron interval. The gap is retained
+  exactly for endpoint evaluation.
+- D: the cubic collision bound is not shown sharp. The four-vertex example
+  proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient; it is not a
+  matching lower bound for the sampling budget.

+def interior_no_gap_standard_zeta_audit() -> dict[str, object]:
+    """Check interior regularity when a binary twisted block has no strict gap."""
+    z = sp.Symbol("z")
+    sample = sp.Rational(1, 3)
+
+    first_identity = sp.Matrix(((2,),))
+    first_involution = sp.zeros(1)
+    second_identity = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    second_involution = sp.Matrix(((1,),))
+    first_base = first_identity + first_involution
+    second_base = second_identity + second_involution
+    first_twisted = first_identity - first_involution
+    second_twisted = second_identity - second_involution
+    first_cover = first_identity.row_join(first_involution).col_join(
+        first_involution.row_join(first_identity)
+    )
+    second_cover = second_identity.row_join(second_involution).col_join(
+        second_involution.row_join(second_identity)
+    )
+
+    same_base_compatible = first_base == second_base
+    perron_root = max(abs(value) for value in first_base.eigenvals())
+    first_twisted_radius = max(abs(value) for value in first_twisted.eigenvals())
+
+    first_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * first_twisted).det())
+    second_determinant = sp.expand((sp.eye(1) - z * second_twisted).det())
+    determinant_ratio = sp.cancel(first_determinant / second_determinant)
+    first_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * first_cover).det())
+    second_cover_zeta = sp.cancel(1 / (sp.eye(2) - z * second_cover).det())
+    standard_zeta_ratio = sp.cancel(second_cover_zeta / first_cover_zeta)
+
+    entrywise_dominated = all(
+        abs(twisted[i, j]) <= first_base[i, j]
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+    parity_compatible = all(
+        (twisted[i, j] - first_base[i, j]) % 2 == 0
+        for twisted in (first_twisted, second_twisted)
+        for i in range(first_base.rows)
+        for j in range(first_base.cols)
+    )
+
+    # Here H(t)=1-2t.  For every j>=0, 0<sample^(2^j)<=sample<1/2,
+    # hence every dyadic factor lies in (0,1).  Its logarithm is negative,
+    # and the positive weighted sum is therefore strictly negative.
+    exact_dyadic_form = determinant_ratio == 1 - 2 * z
+    all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one = bool(
+        exact_dyadic_form and 0 < sample < sp.Rational(1, 2)
+    )
+
+    return {
+        "perron_root": perron_root,
+        "first_twisted_radius": first_twisted_radius,
+        "first_has_strict_gap": first_twisted_radius < perron_root,
+        "sample_radius": sample,
+        "sample_is_interior": sample < 1 / perron_root,
+        "same_base_compatible": same_base_compatible,
+        "entrywise_dominated": entrywise_dominated,
+        "parity_compatible": parity_compatible,
+        "determinants_positive_at_sample": all(
+            polynomial.subs(z, sample) > 0
+            for polynomial in (first_determinant, second_determinant)
+        ),
+        "determinant_ratio": determinant_ratio,
+        "standard_zeta_ratio": standard_zeta_ratio,
+        "determinant_ratio_is_standard_zeta_ratio": (
+            determinant_ratio == standard_zeta_ratio
+        ),
+        "all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+        "dyadic_logarithm_is_negative": (
+            all_dyadic_factors_lie_between_zero_and_one
+        ),
+    }

+\begin{proposition}[Standard zeta interpretation in the binary case]
+\label{prop:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+Let \(G=C_2\), write \(A=A_e+A_s\) for the matrices counting edges with
+labels \(e\) and \(s\), and put \(B=A_e-A_s\).  The adjacency matrix of the
+standard two-sheeted skew-product edge shift is
+\[
+ \widetilde A_\tau=
+ \begin{pmatrix}A_e&A_s\\ A_s&A_e\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+Its Artin--Mazur zeta function satisfies
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}
+ \zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)
+ =\det(I-z\widetilde A_\tau)^{-1}
+ =\frac{1}{\det(I-zA)\det(I-zB)}.
+\end{equation}
+Consequently, for two binary labellings \(\tau,\tau'\) on the same marked
+base, with sign blocks \(B,B'\),
+\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}
+ \frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}
+ =\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}
+        {\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)}.
+\end{equation}
+Thus the rational function used in the binary inverse theorem is a ratio of
+standard dynamical zeta functions, not an additional invariant.
+\end{proposition}
+
+\begin{proof}
+The change of basis
+\((u,v)\mapsto(u+v,u-v)\) conjugates \(\widetilde A_\tau\) over \(\QQ\) to
+\(A\oplus B\).  Taking determinants gives
+\eqref{eq:c2-cover-zeta-factorization}.  The common base determinant cancels
+for \(\tau\) and \(\tau'\), giving \eqref{eq:c2-standard-zeta-ratio}.
+\end{proof}
+

   \phi=\sum_{\rho\in\Irr(G)}

**Outcome**

The paper does not solve a named open problem. I integrated a genuine route-(C) hypothesis removal and a route-(B) identification with standard dynamical zeta functions. Full sources and search records are in the [literature audit](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/artifacts/tier2_literature_audit.md:1).

**Named Problems**

1. Boyle–Schmieding, “Finite group extensions of shifts of finite type: K-theory, Parry and Livsic,” ETDS 37 (2017), DOI `10.1017/etds.2015.87`, Realization Problem 6.1(2): “Given a finite abelian group \(G\), characterize the polynomials \(\det(I-tA)\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\).”
Mapping: our determinant lifting theorem analyzes already-realized same-base matrices; it does not characterize positivity or realizability.

2. Boyle–Schmieding, ibid., Problem 6.1(3): “Given a finite group \(G\), characterize the trace series \(T_A\) and conjugate trace series \(\kappa T_A\) arising from \(G\)-primitive matrices \(A\) over \(\mathbb ZG\).”
Mapping: our Fourier and primitive-orbit formulas recover realized trace/class data but supply no necessary-and-sufficient realization criterion.

3. Chyzak–Dreyfus–Dumas–Mezzarobba, “Computing solutions of linear Mahler equations,” Math. Comp. 87 (2018), DOI `10.1090/mcom/3359`, §4.3: “This result leaves open the question of devising algorithms for computing solutions of linear Mahler equations that run in polynomial time in \(r\) and \(d\), for all possible combinations of these parameters, even when the trailing coefficient \(\ell_0\) of the equation is zero.”
Mapping: our finite Padé algorithm handles one normalized nonlinear order-one coboundary equation, not arbitrary linear Mahler equations or all order-degree regimes.

4. O’Hare, “Finite data rigidity for one-dimensional expanding maps,” ETDS 45 (2025), DOI `10.1017/etds.2024.83`, Introduction: “It would be interesting to study finite data rigidity (Theorem 1.3 below) for unimodal and Markov maps as well.”
Mapping: our theorem concerns symbolic orbit-class Euler values, not periodic derivative data; no distortion or coding argument transfers it to O’Hare’s setting.

Searches covered arXiv/full texts, Crossref, zbMATH, later Mahler papers, and printed open-problem sections. Exact-title and phrase searches found no resolution; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned HTTP 429, so “still open” is the best-supported status, not a proof of non-resolution.

**B/C/D Audit And Result**

B: the binary determinant ratio is now proved to be canonically
\[
\frac{\det(I-zB)}{\det(I-zB')}=
\frac{\zeta_{\widetilde X_{\tau'}}(z)}{\zeta_{\widetilde X_\tau}(z)},
\]
a ratio of standard Artin–Mazur zeta functions of two-sheeted SFT covers; see [the proposition](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/sec_refocused_framework.tex:175).

C was chosen for the best success-impact product. Entrywise domination proves \(\rho(B),\rho(B')\leq\lambda\), so for every algebraic \(0<y<\lambda^{-1}\), the collision condition is equivalent to a unique rational Mahler certificate without any strict twisted gap; see [the lifting theorem](/D:/omega/automath/papers/publication/2026_finite_parts_dynamical_zeta_shifts_finite_type_etds/sec_refocused_boundary_collisions.tex:451).

Consequently, fewer than \(16v^3\) interior algebraic samples recover every binary primitive length-class profile unconditionally. General finite-group recovery from any radial set with an interior accumulation point is also unconditional. The strict gap remains only for evaluating at \(y=\lambda^{-1}\).

The parity hypothesis remains real: it supplies integral Mahler coefficients required by the special-value argument. For \(C_3\), Adams–Möbius inversion couples character determinants at non-lacunary powers, precisely where the one-function Mahler method stops.

D offers no tier-raising result: the cubic sample bound has no matching lower bound, and the four-vertex construction proves only that one Perron-endpoint sample is insufficient. No sharp converse or optimal constant was established.
